r.txt:
8. Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

The Mole

Atoms and molecules are so small that even one gram of a substance contains many trillions of atoms.

To simplify this, chemists measure the quantity of a chemical using a unit called the mole. This term was introduced in 1865 by the chemist August Wilhelm von Hofmann to describe the mass of a molecule, because the Latin term for mass is moles.

Another scientist, Amedeo Avogadro, took this one step further by defining one mole as the number of carbon atoms in 12 g of carbon, where each atom contains six protons and six neutrons. This number, known as Avogadro’s number, is 6.02 × 1023.

For example, one mole of water contains 6.02 × 1023 water molecules.

Avogadro’s number is represented by the letter L. This can be used to calculate the number of atoms in one mole of molecules as shown in the table.

Molecular formulaTotal number of atoms in moleculeNumber of atoms in one mole
HCl22L
NH344L

r.label: Question 6

oe.title: Investigating copper as a catalyst for zinc and sulfuric acid
n5: Run two experiments: zinc + sulfuric acid without copper, and with copper. Keep the mass and particle size of zinc, the acid volume, concentration and temperature the same.
Measure the rate: volume of hydrogen collected over time (gas syringe), or time for the zinc to react, or loss in mass.
If copper is a catalyst, the reaction with copper is faster.
Weigh the copper before and after; a catalyst is recovered chemically unchanged, so the mass stays the same.
Check copper on its own does not react with dilute sulfuric acid (copper is below hydrogen).
higher: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.
Copper and zinc in contact form a simple cell: electrons flow from zinc to copper and hydrogen is released at the copper surface, so the rate increases.
Heterogeneous catalyst: the catalyst (solid) is in a different state from the reactants (solution).
eqns: Rate = 60 cm³ / 30 s = 2 cm³ s⁻¹ (example of comparing average rates)
diagrams: Flask with zinc, acid and copper turnings connected to a gas syringe.
Two curves on one graph: with copper (steeper) and without copper, ending at the same final volume.
Potential energy diagram showing the lower Ea of the catalysed route.

r.label: Question 8

oe.title: The chemistry of water
n5: Covalent molecular compound H₂O: angular (bent) shape; each O-H is a covalent bond.
Good solvent: dissolves ionic compounds (ions free to move) and is used to make solutions.
Neutral (pH 7): contains equal concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻; dilution moves acids and alkalis towards pH 7.
Product of neutralisation and of combustion of hydrocarbons and alcohols; tested with cobalt chloride paper (blue to pink).
Reacts with reactive metals (e.g. sodium) to form alkali + hydrogen; soluble metal oxides and non-metal oxides react with water to form alkalis and acids.
Used in hydration (alkene + water → alcohol) and as the coolant/heat absorber in E = cmΔT experiments (c = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹).
higher: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules (polar O-H bonds, permanent dipoles) explains its unusually high boiling point and why ice is less dense than water.
O is more electronegative than H, so the O-H bonds are polar and the molecule is polar overall.
Hydrolysis: water breaks esters, fats and proteins apart; condensation reactions release water.
Water acts as both acid and base: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ (dynamic equilibrium).
diagrams: Dot-and-cross diagram of H₂O showing two bonding pairs and two non-bonding pairs; angular shape.
Hydrogen bonds drawn as dotted lines between water molecules (delta+ H to delta- O).
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions surrounded by water molecules when dissolving.
